newsitem.title: USA: EU seeks common ground on Boeing deals, official says.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks common ground on Boeing deals, official says.

text.p: A key European official Thursday softened the stance of the European Union against Boeing Co.'s controversial exclusive agreements to provide jetliners to two big airlines.

In another conciliatory move, EU competition official Alexander Schaub said he would try to reach common ground with the Federal Trade Commission in analysing problems with the deals and how they relate to the Boeing's planned merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Schaub, second in command of the EU authority reviewing the $14 billion merger, is visiting Washington for meetings with American antitrust authorities on Friday.

"We will do everything to come to identical views with American authorities on objections to the deal and once we have reached this then we will look into possible remedies," he told reporters after speaking to the European Institute. "And I believe they (the Americans) will do everything also to avoid contradictory conclusions."

The discussions are likely to touch on the exclusive provider agreements, a sore point with the EU. Boeing, already dominant in Europe over the European consortium of Airbus Industrie, has signed the 20-year agreements with Delta Air Lines and American Airlines.
Schaub said the pacts undermined competition and were antitrust rather than trade issues, but he declined to say categorically they would stop the EU from approving the proposed merger.

"Nobody can tell you today what would be the outcome of our European investigation and what will be the outcome of the American investigation here done by the FTC (Federal Trade Commission)," he told an International Monetary Fund meeting.
Those comments stand in contrast to the views Schaub's boss, European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, expressed in April.

"I can't see how possibly we can give our authorisation to the merger with such a system in place," Van Miert said during a visit to Washington on April 18. "To our mind this is something which should be declared illegal. And I have no doubt that, if needed, we are going to do so in the European Union."

Schaub was far more tentative: "You could come to the idea that exclusive deals worsen, particularly long-term exclusive deals, worsen the competitive situation and that without exclusive deals the situation may be perhaps slightly less unacceptable."
The United States has stepped up criticism of the EU review in recent weeks.

Last month U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in The Hague Americans want "assurances that the inquiry must be conducted on competition policy principles and not on extraneous political principles."
Schaub defended the investigation, saying it is in strict compliance with the law.

"We do not consider Boeing to be a case of extraterritorial application of EU merger control laws," he said. "The commission will scrutinise this merger under strictly legal terms." He said the inquiry would not be politicized.

He said the only sure thing at this point is that the EU will meet its July 31 deadline for a decision. The FTC must act 20 business days after Boeing and McDonnell Douglas submit all required paperwork, which Boeing officials said will happen next week.
